utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 13th of October, 2009. I would like to greet our witness. General, the Bench greets you. Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the witness says he's not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear now? Fine. I was saying that I would like to greet you, first and foremost. I would also like to greet the accused - Mr. Pusic, that said, is absent. I assume he's ill. And I would like him -- and wish him a quick recovery - Defence counsel, the OTP members who are here in the courtroom today, as well as all the people assisting us. Mr. Laws' cross-examination will resume, and I shall give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to each of Your Honours and to everyone in and around the courtroom, and good morning to you, Mr. Curcic. Cross-examination by Mr. Laws [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take you back, please, to a document that we were looking at yesterday, P02813, just so that we pick up the thread. P02813. We looked at that yesterday, and you agreed with me that Brigadier Miljenko Lasic appeared to be giving a similar sort of approval to the one that we saw that you gave on the 6th of August. Do you remember we looked at that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, mine was a request, and this is an approval or certificate, confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Just so that we have the full picture, can you turn back three documents to P02240, and I just want to have a look at Miljenko Lasic. This is a document that relates to Mostar. And I'm going to go on to Mostar in a moment; I don't want to deal with Mostar as a topic now. I just want to see Miljenko Lasic, on the 9th of May of 1993, issuing orders to your unit and, in paragraph 4, holding you responsible for the implementation of an order to deploy to Mostar. All right? We're going to deal with Mostar as a topic separately, but what I want to glean from that document now is this: He was in your chain of command, the gentleman who issued the request or approval in P02813, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I arrived in Mostar a day earlier, and I was subordinated to the operative zone in South-East Herzegovina, and so Mr. Miljenko Lasic had the right to be my commanding officer because I was already under his command from the 9th onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the South-East Herzegovina zone of operations, and he was a superior officer to you, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my superior officer for the time being because of the events that were happening. Before [as interpreted] the 9th, I was re-subordinated to Mr. Miljenko Lasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him? Was he somebody with whom you met and conversed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but for the record, a correction to the record. The witness didn't say "before the 9th," that he was re-subordinated before the 9th, but he said that he was re-subordinated "on the 9th." So I want to put that right in the record. And it is page 3, line 7. So on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was somebody who you met and who you spoke to. Did the two of you ever discuss these requests or approvals that you both issued, exempting or asking for certain individuals to be treated in a specific way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Lasic issued an approval. I never issued approvals. I wrote requests, I wrote a request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know I'm going to suggest to you, which is precisely what I'm asking you: Did you and he discuss the approvals, or requests, or whatever you want to call them, efforts to exempt certain specific people from what was happening in the Stolac and Capljina municipalities? Did you and he ever discuss that as a topic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can we turn and look at P04044.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 9th of August of 1993. It relates to Rama. It's signed by Ilija Franjic, the military police commander, and it's called a "Ban on harassment" as its subject. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at any time deployed in this area in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not quite sure. It is possible because I was in the area of Prozor-Rama fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You were in Prozor and Rama quite often, including in the summer of 1993, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can't say for sure. It is highly possible. I know for sure that I was there in April, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have look at --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at what the document says: "Ban on harassment. "The consent is given that the family of Mihad Kulaglic must not be prosecuted, or detained by no means, nor expelled from the house because that gentleman is engaged in the Rama Brigade units ..." And: "The consent is said to be valid until further notice or its revocation." Again, I'm going to suggest to you that rather a similar request is being made to the one that you made and the one that Mr. Lasic made to exempt a particular individual for a particular reason. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor, why he was asking for this. I don't know. The person who compiled this document is Ilija Franjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It tells us why he's being exempted, because he's in the Rama Brigade. It's precisely the same reason that Fatima Klepo was exempted because Senad Klepo was in the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion. It's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is approval or agreement to the ban on harassment, so something that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what can you tell us about the events in Prozor-Rama in the summer of 1993 that might lead to somebody needing to be exempted from being persecuted, or detained, or expelled from their house? Was that something that was going on in that area that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in Rama, from the beginning of the conflict until the truce between the Croats and Bosniaks, there were daily clashes. And in those daily clashes, the civilians would flee towards territory where they felt safer, and those who stayed on perhaps had some problems. And you must know and be aware of the fact that due to killings and woundings, some members might take it upon themselves to retaliate. But here we have in Rama the Rama Brigade and this agreement on the ban on harassment, so I don't actually know what Mr. Franjic wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn on, with me, please, in the binder to P06002. It's a document from October of 1993, signed by Ivica Lucic. Just take a moment to read that, if you would, please, Mr. Curcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a request that there be protection for the apartment of Mr. Hadziosmanovic in Mostar. Again, you and your battalion spent time in Mostar. Were you aware that events in Mostar required that individuals had their apartments put under protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there's no mention here of me or my unit. What is requested is that the military police provide security. I see no reason -- well, since I was in Mostar at the time, although I don't think I was in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion certainly went to Mostar several times, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the events that you saw in Mostar give you any insight into why the military police would need to protect a flat of a Muslim male who had certain political views? Did you see what was going on in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it says in this document, very specifically, what it was about. It says: "Because of increased tension in town, we consider that protection and security is necessary 'round the clock." So this has been established in this document. How should I know whether the man actually needed protection or not, regardless of the fact that I came into Mostar with my unit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you whether you thought he needed protection; I'm asking you whether you saw things in Mostar. And I asked you the same question about Prozor-Rama and about Stolac-Capljina, whether you saw things in Mostar that accorded with this sentiment that certain individuals needed to be protected from what was going on. Did you see such events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me a general question. If I was somewhere, and then you asked me about some specific event and quote a date, so it's very difficult for me to put together an answer. Let's talk about the 22nd of October, for instance, when this document was compiled. Obviously, the assistant minister here assessed the need for 'round-the-clock protection for this man, and most probably there was reason for him making that decision. I can't say why an assistant minister is writing something or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I haven't, with respect, Mr. Curcic, asked you to try to say why he should write anything. I'm asking you whether in these locations that we're looking at you saw things going on that accorded with the need to protect individuals, for orders or requests to be made asking for protection to be afforded to certain individuals. Did you see -- let's take Mostar, for example. Did you see people or hear about people having their flats broken into, looted, people being taken away, or forced out at gunpoint? Did you see events or hear of events of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've got about five questions there, but let me try and answer. Flats were broken into as soon as the JNA officers left them, and both Croats and Muslims broke into them. Now, when the conflict began between the Croats and Bosniaks, the first thing that happened as a result was that the civilians fled, because civilians always flee from a site where there's fighting going on. So if people wanted to find safety and security in areas controlled either by the HVO or the BH Army, then, once again, flats would be left vacant and people would take up accommodation in them and break into them. So I, personally, wasn't present, what you're asking me about, whether somebody broke into the flats or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that the picture that emerges from the documents that we've looked at is a campaign of persecution of the Muslim population. That's the first thing. What do you say about that? The Muslim population were being persecuted month after month after month, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know the exact number of Muslims who stayed on in Mostar, but I do know that the figure is a large one. That certain people were persecuted, that is possible, but I do know that lots of Muslims stayed on in the area of Mostar under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, first of all, let me say good morning to everybody. I let the witness answer. I didn't want to interrupt the examination, but I do have to step in for the transcript because in the document last shown by the Prosecutor, which is P60002, it says, quite clearly, why protection is being sought, political -- or, rather, protection for a rather important political figure, as it says here, and he was the president of the Muslim Democratic Party in Mostar. So it's a document which, in peacetime, is also customary. Or, rather, it's a step taken in peacetime, because in peacetime, too, flats of important political figures are protected. And here in this document, it is stated why this protection is being sought, because of a killing that had taken place, the murder. And so that's what I wanted to say with regard to the last question asked by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, there was no need to step in, because the Judges have read the document and we see why this doctor is being protected, the president of the SDA, Hadziosmanovic, because someone has been killed prior to that, a Croat Muslim has been killed. So perhaps the Dr. Hadziosmanovic was also for the Croats. We don't know. So in October, this man is being protected. This is what the document states. The Prosecutor is addressing another topic, so let him take the floor and let him address the topic he wishes to address. He's going to put questions to the witness. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for intervening, but I think there should be a correction to the transcript to avoid further misunderstanding. On page 8, line 14, it says here that the witness's answer was: [In English] "Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know the exact number of the Muslims who stayed on in Mostar, but I do know that the figure is a large one." [Interpretation] End of quotation. That is completely incorrect. I'm quite sure -- could the witness be asked to repeat? The witness said, I don't know the exact number of Muslims who stayed on in West Mostar, but I do know that the number was great. Quite a different qualification. Perhaps it's best for him to repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what did you say, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know the exact number, but I do know that there were many of them who stayed on in the part of town which was under the control of the Croats. And when I say that, I mean the Bosniak Muslims I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn on with me, please, to document P09 -- P09847, which is a document under seal, Mr. President. This document is going to take us back to what was actually happening in Capljina and Stolac in the summer of 1993. And when you find the document, Mr. Curcic, you'll find that in the B/C/S there's a little number in the bottom right-hand corner. You're looking for a little "4 of 6." And in the English, it's page 2, halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number of the document, please? What did you say, 09 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness is having much luck with the binder. Could he perhaps have a hand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, if you look in the bottom right-hand corner of the B/C/S, Mr. Curcic, you'll see there are numbers. If you find number 4 of 6 and look at the very top of the page, you'll find the paragraph that I want to direct your attention to. It starts: "On the 13th of July ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: " ... women, children, and old people (the men were already detained since a week) from seven villages between Stolac and Capljina, at least 420 people, were ordered by HVO soldiers to climb six army trucks immediately." You read the rest of that paragraph to yourself, we'll read it too, and then in just a moment I'll ask you to read another short paragraph. Tell us when you finish that one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you come down three paragraphs from where you are, you'll see, on the B/C/S, just next to the black rectangle to the right of the page, there's a two-line paragraph: "The evictions and rounding up of people, including the women, children, and old people, have been violent with threats and shooting over their heads." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to suggest to you is that when you wrote about Ms. Klepo being exempted from ill treatment and being taken away, this was precisely what you had in mind, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote a letter on the 6th of August asking that Fatima Klepo from Capljina be exempted from taking away and ill treatment, this that we've just looked at, that was actually happening in your area, was precisely what you had in mind, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you there. As for Ms. Klepo, I wrote it following a request from her son. Now, I know that soldiers did arrest people; we've already been through that. And also these expulsions of the 13th, I wasn't there, I wasn't present, so I don't know what happened, that there was shooting above civilians' heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We have a major mistake in the transcript and interpretation. On page 12, line 6 -- no, line 5, the witness said, "I know that soldiers were arrested." And the interpretation was: "I know that soldiers arrested people." Perhaps it would be a good idea if the witness were to repeat what he said so that we can see if I'm right or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Witness. Can you specify what it was exactly you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that soldiers and possible conscripts were arrested. I don't know that women and children were arrested or where they would go with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August, the internationals - as we've just seen in that document - the United Nations knew what was going on in your municipality, and you're saying to us that you didn't. Is that it, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, precisely on the morning of the 13th of July, there was a strong diversionary attack throughout the Dubrava Plateau conducted by sabotage groups, members of the previous Croatian Defence Council who had joined the BH Army, or, rather, previous members of the HVO who'd joined the BH Army. And I took part from the early morning of the 13th and over the next four or five days until the lines had been fully established, the defence lines, I mean. I know that for a fact, because on the 13th, in those -- in that fighting that went on the whole day and the following day, and over the next few days, three of my men were killed, and two exactly on the 13th: Bule, and one man called Ivankovic from Visici. So when you're asking me now that some people did some shooting, I don't know that. But where we were fighting, all the civilians had fled, all the civilians who were both Croats and Bosniaks, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, were you talking about the 13th of June now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I just verify because this document does not refer to the date of 13 July. It refers to 13 of June, at least in the version I have. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, if I might be of assistance. The Prosecutor started his question referring to this document, and on the second page of this document, the ERN number being R003-6133, and in paragraph 5 on that page, the paragraph begins with the 13th of July. It says "the 13th of July," and that was precisely what the Prosecutor based his question on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry, I got stuck in the second paragraph of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a follow-up question for you. I have listened carefully to what you told us about what happened on the Dubrava Plateau. You explained to us that you spent several days fighting, and three of your soldiers were killed. Right. In the document we have before us, it says the following: "On 13th of July, 420 people are arrested, and these people are then taken to the silo building in Capljina, where these people are going to be detained for three days." Since you weren't there, it is practically sure that you did not know that these 420 people were detained. But in the document, at the end of the document, it states that on the 22nd or 23rd of July, this group of people was taken elsewhere, to Doljani and Jablanica. And then, three days later, another group was transported to the front-line area, and you remained on the Dubrava Plateau for several days. But when you returned to Capljina, if you returned on the 18th or 19th of July, the people left on the 22nd of July, so for a few days you may have seen or heard about the fact that civilians were there. Is that possible or totally impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is quite possible. I told you it was about four to five days when I and part of the command returned to Capljina, and we certainly did for one day in order to attend the burials of these members. But the fighting went on for I don't know exactly how many days, and when I returned with the unit to the barrack in Capljina, I did not find -- I didn't see anyone there. I know, and I repeat it, that there were arrests of military conscripts, but whether women and children were taken away, I really don't know because I was in the area where the conflict was going on and there were no women and children there. So in the town itself, I didn't see these trucks or these people who were taken -- transported to Doljani, because I know where Doljani, near Jablanica, is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I know that you were born in Zenica, and you must have known that at the same time Croats were detained in Zenica. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You knew it. Very well. Did you know that the rule was to exchange civilians from one side to the other? This was a common practice, and the international community knew this very well, that civilians were exchanged. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that war -- prisoners of war, both members of the HVO and the BH Army, were exchanged mutually. I do know that columns of refugees did came to Bosnia and Herzegovina because there were a lot of people I knew there. As I was telling you, the people from the Capljina area, the civilians, had moved out, but how and when, I don't know because I didn't -- I wasn't there. But at the time when there were daily clashes and fighting between the BH Army and the HVO, as one or the other side took over control over a certain area, so as one side or the other took control over a certain area, then the civilian population that was not from that ethnic group would move out and go to the territory that was under the control of their army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, earlier we saw a document where the civilians, women and children, were brought together, sometimes were abused; and in order for things to happen smoothly, people were shooting over their heads. According to you, is this proper military conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that kind of treatment would not be in compliance with military duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last question about this topic, and then we're going to turn to something else. Do you know if Fatima Klepo managed to avoid being ill-treated and taken away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know, or she didn't manage to survive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I never met that person afterward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that. But her son, who you say had asked you to write this letter for reasons you're not fully aware of, he didn't ever come to you and say that there'd been a problem with his mother?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the sort of thing that a commanding officer learns from his soldiers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never learned that from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, overnight I thought of a question for you, and the Prosecutor is giving me an opportunity for this: Could you tell me whether Senad Klepo stayed in your unit throughout the entire time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Senad Klepo and his brother left. And as far as I know, they left -- they went abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they leave right after making this request, soon after making this request, or a long time after that? Maybe they left because, after having seen that their mother was not protected, they lost trust in your unit and left. Could you tell us when they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know. This can be verified through the records, the unit records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question, another question I thought of overnight: Could you tell us how many men were in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the manpower -- the unit manpower would vary anywhere between 192 members, and that's the number of us that came to Herzegovina, up until the end when there were up to 350 members. At this time, I was no longer a commander. But all the unit members were not registered immediately, nor were contracts drawn up with them, so this is something that we would have to check, to look at the map of the unit structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question: During your period of command, could you tell us how many of your men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In total, the unit numbered -- the unit had 34 men -- lost 34 men, 34 were killed. And while I was in command, I think there were 21 dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, let's start a new topic. Shall we look, please, together at the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion, and start with a document in your binder, P02632. And this appears to be a document written by you on the 4th of June of 1993. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not the author of this document. You can see at the bottom that it said "for Ferdo Herceg."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has, at the bottom, your name typed, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Ludvig Pavlovic-headed letter paper, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. But you can see, next to my name --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. And it has a stamp at the bottom - does it not? - through the name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were going to tell us someone else has signed it on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can explain this document. However, I did not sign it. Ferdo Herceg, my deputy, signed it, and you can see that on the document. It says there are four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, I would just like to point out a matter -- an issue with interpretation, and this is why the Prosecutor suggested to the witness that he had signed it. The translation of the document does not contain the word "for," which can be found in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I said that he was the author of it, not that he signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nevertheless, the translation is not in compliance -- is not -- does not accord with the original, because in the original it says that this was signed "for" the unit commander and not "by" the unit commander. So that is my remark or note that has to do with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's noted on the transcript, this document was not signed by this person, but by someone else. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you read with me, please, the paragraph below the word "receipt" in the middle of the page. Would you just read the first paragraph aloud for us so we can be clear about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Receipt confirming that Mr. Zlatko Brajkovic, son of Drago, born on 8th January, 1954, in Zvirovici, Capljina municipality, residing in Capljina, is a member of this unit which ..." Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... which has the status of an independent unit with -- pursuant to an order by the minister of defence, Mr. Gojko Susak, as stipulated in Article 47, paragraph 5, of the Law on Defence (Official Gazette 49/91, 53A ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The receipt was issued upon the request of the aforementioned for the purpose of regulating rights and duties."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The words that you seem to have left out, according to my translation, after "independent unit" are "independent unit within the Croatian Army." Is that not in the original?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it may well be just there's an error in translation. But this document is saying that Mr. Brajkovic is a member of the Ludvig Pavlovic Special-Purpose Unit, which has the status of an independent unit within the Croatian Army, according to an order of Mr. Susak. That's what the document's saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with that assessment of the standing of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two units. We're talking about two units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you better tell us about the two units. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Herzegovina from the 1st Volunteer Regiment, Kralj Tomislav, 92 members had a contract with the Croatian Army; whereas the other members who joined our unit when we arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina had the status of members -- or as members of the Croatian Defence Council. Those of us who had the status as members of the Croatian Army did not wish to relinquish that status because of the salaries that we were getting and also health insurance and other types of insurance that we were getting as benefits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you remained a unit of the Croatian Army, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Daidza, who was our commander of the Kralj Tomislav unit, he set up a new unit, which had its headquarters in Vrgorac, so that the status-related matters could be resolved, the status-related matters of members of the one-time Kralj Tomislav unit. But this did not apply to those members who were not members of the Croatian Army, as we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. If we accept for a moment that only some of you were members of the Croatian Army, and we try to look at what you're describing, you had a contract with the Croatian Army. You've just told us that you didn't want to relinquish that because of the salary, the health insurance, and other types of insurance that you were getting as benefits. You're describing a unit that remained part of the Croatian Army, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how are you not a member of the Croatian Army if you're being -- you have a contract with them, you're paid by them, and they give you health and other benefits? In what way are you not a member of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that I was a member of the Croatian Army, but you were asking about the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were the commander.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us individuals -- I was the commander of the Ludvig Pavlovic unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And this gentleman that we're talking about on this document, Zlatko Brajkovic, he -- does he have the same arrangements as you, contract with the Croatian Army, paid by the Croatian Army, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatko Brajkovic is currently a disabled veteran in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Curcic, but you couldn't try to make up an answer less relevant to the question that I've just asked you than that. To tell us what he's doing now, you know that that's not attempting to be helpful. Would you look at the question. I'm -- is it right that you actually speak quite good English as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for that. But, look, the question that I've asked you is quite a straightforward one. Zlatko Brajkovic, does he have the same arrangement with you, a contract with the Croatian Army, paid by the Croatian Army, et cetera; is that right? At this time, not now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have a contract with the Croatian Army, and he did have -- he did receive pay from the HV, and this is further confirmed by his present status, where he has the status of a disabled veteran of the Army of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of this document, then, that you say correctly isn't signed by you, what part of it don't you agree with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I asked you a little while ago whether you agreed with the contents of this document, and you told us that you did not, and that's why I've spent some time looking at its details to try to see whether it's right or not, and I'm asking you again. The document, with your name on your unit's note paper, accurately reflects the position, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first of all, we said that I was not the one who drafted the document and that this document was signed by my deputy, but I am prepared to explain everything as if I were the author. As far as I'm concerned, this receipt is quite in order because a member of the unit is asking for something for the purpose of regulating his status-related matters. So he is the one who is submitting this request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's quite in order because it describes him as being a member of the unit which has the status of an independent unit within the Croatian Army. That part of it is also right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I've explained that this unit was a unit of the Croatian Army earlier and not this one here that was signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must be my fault. You've lost me there. This is dated the 4th of June of 1993, this document. Are you saying that the arrangement that it describes is no longer in force in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when the Kralj Tomislav unit, under the command of General Daidza, when it was disbanded, when it fell apart and came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, its members -- we set up a new unit, Ludvig Pavlovic; whereas in Konjic, a Nihad -- a unit called Nihad Konjevic was established. All the members who had had a contract with the Croatian Army had this contract through the unit of General Sarlija, Daidza. And it was through this unit that they were able to enjoy all the rights that they had in the Republic of Croatia, because Daidza, General Mate Sarlija, organised the military post in Vrgorac through which it was possible to regulate one status-related matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Are you saying that the arrangement that this document describes is no longer in force in June of 1993 or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which arrangement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arrangement under which the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, or, if you like, some of its members, were an independent unit within the Croatian Army. Was that the position in June of 1993 or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1993, Mr. Zlatko Brajkovic was a member of the Croatian Army, and he was serving in the Ludvig Pavlovic unit in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was requesting here to have his status resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that is perfectly satisfactory for my purposes. Shall we turn on, please, to another document dealing with the Ludvig Pavlovic, P08107. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... my colleague. I apologise, but I was waiting for another topic to come up. I've just discovered, in view of the reiterated reply by the witness, that there was an error in the transcript on page 17, line 20. Your Honour, you asked him then what the number -- the manpower was in the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, and in the transcript, on page 17, line 20, it says "between 192, at the least, in the beginning," and to me I thought even then that the witness had said "92," but I wasn't sure. However, a few moments ago, on page 20, line 25, the witness again repeated this number, and this time he said that there were 92 men who came from Vrgorac to Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of this unit. So maybe we should clear this up, whether the figure was actually 192 or 92. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when I asked you what the manpower was in the unit, it was complete manpower. I didn't make a difference between those who had a contract with the HV and those who didn't. Now, you answered by saying at least 192 and up to -- all the way to 350. Does this -- is this valid for the entire unit, all categories included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not 190, it is 92. But as time went on, the number increased, and at one point it numbered even 350 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ninety-two was the figure you started with, and the unit ended with 350 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good, that's very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn with me, please, to P08107 [Realtime transcript read in error "P08178"] you have it already, I think. Good. Is this a document that you have written and signed, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's dated the 23rd of March of 1994, and it's addressed to the Chief of the Main Staff of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, General Bobetko, personally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the first two lines of this letter: "We are referring to you, as our direct commander, with a request for assistance to solve payment of personal wages to members of our battalion." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it goes on to talk about problems that have arisen with you being paid, and comparing Croatian payments to HVO payments. But the phrase I want to look at with you, please, is this: "We are referring to you as our direct commander." Was General Bobetko your direct commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my direct commander -- or, rather, direct commander Janko Bobetko was the commander of Sarlija, and through him down to us for the resolution of issues of status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible to answer that question "yes" or "no"? Was Mr. Bobetko, General Bobetko, your direct commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can give you a more extensive answer with respect to this document, which was compiled in Vrgorac, which is a town in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure and I'm certain that you could do that. But I've asked you the question whether it's possible for you to say whether Mr. Bobetko was your direct commander, as you address him in this document. Was he your direct commander, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never -- Mr. Bobetko never issued any orders to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a question quite different from the one that I've asked you. Was General Bobetko your direct commander, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, do you address him as being your direct commander? It would strike - wouldn't it? - most objective readers as rather odd, to write someone a letter, calling them something which they know they're not. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why on earth do you call him something that he isn't? Did you get a letter back saying, Why are you calling me your direct commander; what's going on down there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: If you look at the subject matter, it refers to paying out salaries to the men who came from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've seen that, but that doesn't alter how you address him, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kneel before him, if necessary, for me to get the salaries for my men. But you have to know that this document was compiled with General Daidza, who at the time was stronger than General Bobetko. He was more respected, more highly respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you telling us about your willingness to kneel before him? Are you saying that this is in some way you praising him or attempting to get into his good books by calling him your direct commander; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to get the salaries for my men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it help you, to get your salaries, to call him by a title that isn't his? Just help me with that. Why make up a title for him that doesn't belong to him in order to try to get salaries? It's quite a confusing thing to try to understand, Mr. Curcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the 1st Volunteer Regiment was put up in Vrgorac. When we went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Mate Sarlija stayed on in Vrgorac. It was through General Mate Sarlija that we resolved all our issues of status with respect to the Croatian Army. And as you can see in this particular document, it was compiled in Vrgorac on the 23rd of March, not in Capljina, with the clear objective of trying to ensure enough monies for our men. But Mr. Bobetko never commanded us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We have your answer on that. Would you look with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Laws. It's just for the -- about the record. On page 26, line 2, the number of this document is indicated as P08178. In my bundle, at least, it has the number P08107.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That is its correct number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we've already interrupted the proceedings, a correction to the transcript. I don't know if it was a mistake or not, but I think the witness gave the full date. I'm referring to page 28, line 16. It's still on our screens. The witness said that the document was compiled in Vrgorac on the 23rd of March, I believe. And I think he added "1994," but that follows from the document. So it's a good idea to have the full date there with the year, not only the day of the month, and that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, I was going to put a question to you which should settle this issue. This letter is addressed to General Bobetko, personally, and dated the 23rd of March, 1994. I haven't looked at the English; I only looked at the B/C/S version. Clearly, this is a document which leaves the ministry post, 3280, which is in the purview of the Croatian Army, so this document stems from the Croatian Army. And you explain in this letter that there are problems regarding the payment of the soldiers. You even say that you have been told that from February onwards they would have 1.200.000 dinars per soldier, which is 700.000 less than what the soldiers receive in the Croatian Army. So there is a problem regarding the payment of the salaries of the Croatian soldiers. And this document comes from the Croatian Army. And we know that you are attached to the HVO. And you suggest that this be paid by the district in Split or by the battle-field in the south. So you were confronted with the payment of the salaries of the soldiers. That said, in your mind, did this mean that the Croatian Army was deployed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did this mean that volunteers in the Croatian Army had gone to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to serve in the HVO? What was the situation exactly, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When talking about us, we all left as individuals to the Croatian Defence Council, 92 of us, the first lot, and then we were joined by many others in Herzegovina. We wanted, at all costs, to retain our status in the Croatian Army because of salaries and other benefits. And everything that we had to deal with, we dealt with our -- with our immediate commander, because he was the sole person responsible to deal with our needs with respect to personnel matters and financial matters. And our commander was Mate Sarlija, Daidza, our immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you personally, if someone had told you that you were part of the HVO Army and you will be paid by the HVO, and your contract with the Croatian Army is terminated, would you have then gone over to the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we moved to the HVO, it wasn't something that was a big question. The salaries weren't that large. But in the ensuing period, it was important to retain your status in the Croatian Army. But, yes, I would certainly have stayed on in the HVO to fight, even were things different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to interrupt you, but you have said that if someone had told you that you would be paid by the HVO, "I would nonetheless have joined the HVO." That is what you're telling us, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but this is what I said and thought: If I had to choose either to receive a salary from Croatia, if I left the HVO, or to stay on in the HVO while the fighting was going on, I would have stayed on in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you have stated that you all went to Herceg-Bosna voluntarily as individuals. I find it difficult to reconcile this with the fact that you have here a letterhead printed, I suppose, where the top line reads -- there's an abbreviation that I cannot identify, but "Samas Dama Vojna HV [phoen]." That is not 92 individuals or something like that, that is Ludvig Pavlovic, a unit. How do you reconcile? You say, We are all individuals, and then you write on a letterhead of a unit, which the letterhead said it's a unit of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this military post in Vrgorac, registered by General Mate Sarlija, Daidza, and the name of the unit dealt with us Croats and the Bosniaks who were with us in the Kralj Tomislav unit and who made requests for having their status in Croatia resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look with us, please, at a document that you were given yesterday in this separate binder, which is headed "4D Documents, Witness Dragan Curcic." Do you remember getting that? It's a bundle of documents you were given before I gave you my bundle. It's not that one. Does that say "4D" on the inside cover?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "4D." What number, 4D --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 4D00618. And this was the organisational chart that you were looking at yesterday, and you identified the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion on the left-hand side, with a dotted line leading to the Main Staff, under a heading "Chart of the HVO Structure." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this fair? To be more accurate, this chart should have a line connecting the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion to General Mate Sarlija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military post, military post Vrgorac, linking this, whereas this is the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, made up of men who had come from the Croatian Army, but also of those who joined us up and had nothing to do with the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion should be subdivided, so that the chart is clearer, with one part having a line connecting it to General Mate Sarlija. Would that be more accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this chart shows the special units of the Croatian Defence Council, special-purpose units, which is where Ludvig Pavlovic belongs, too. Now, the military post, 3280 Vrgorac, was registered in Vrgorac in order to resolve status issues for members of the HV from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The question that I'm asking you is whether it would be more accurate for this chart to show part of the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion with a dotted line leading to General Mate Sarlija, or General Bobetko, or another figure, if you like, within the Croatian Army. That would show us - wouldn't it? - that the full structure that related to the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wouldn't show that. This chart shows us who can, in operational terms, deploy the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, who can use it; and the military post in Vrgorac serves to resolve the issues of status of its members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were on loan from Croatia; that's what it comes down to, isn't it? You were on loan from Croatia, being funded by Croatia, and you were there in Herceg-Bosna to assist the HVO; that's the long and the short of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an ugly expression, "loan." All of us -- well, not all of us, but 90 per cent of us were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we originated from there, and we went to the Republic of Croatia voluntarily, to fight as volunteers, both Croats and Bosniaks. Now, when the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we felt the need to return, and that's what we did. We went back, and we made a large contribution, we Croats and the Bosniaks, first of all together, jointly, and then individually in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it was from our Bosniaks that the best units of the BH Army were formed. And some members were able to resolve their status in the RH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ludvig Pavlovic were some of the best soldiers that the HVO had at their disposal, weren't they? I don't mean to flatter you, but that was the simple position, wasn't it; well trained, well armed, good fighters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a significant asset of the HVO Main Staff, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a unit which could be deployed speedily and to effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you were sometimes deployed to lead an attack? Sometimes you were deployed to lead an attack in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever we took part in attack operations, we were the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And sometimes you were deployed in response to difficulties that had arisen. Where the enemy had gained ground or made advances, they'd call in the Ludvig Pavlovic to fill the gap, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes reinforcing other HVO units that had not found it easy to hold their own or had met unexpected opposition; that's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to turn, then, to consider Mostar and your unit's involvement in Mostar in May of 1993. Can you just help us with the day that you were first deployed to Mostar? Was it on Sunday, the 9th of May, or Monday, the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Sunday. Well, I think it was the 9th, and all the documents indicate that it was the 9th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vranica building fell on the 10th, and you were there when that happened, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So had you been deployed the day before that and spent the night in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd gone there on the 9th, and what had you done on the 9th of May? What action had the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade been involved in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Combat action in Mostar. Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the Vranica building, the School of Economics, around the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were to be engaged in combat around the Vranica building the following day as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat action went on continuously until the Vranica building was taken control of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the Vranica building was the headquarters of the 4th Corps, and, in particular, the basement of that building was theirs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not - was it? - a building of otherwise strategic importance. It didn't command a significant view over Mostar, unlike, for example, the hills around Mostar; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's where you were deployed -- the best troops were deployed to attack the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its headquarters in order to take it; that's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived down there not to attack, but to prevent their attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, their attack, I'm going to suggest to you, was nothing but a response to yours. And you were attacking, largely, a building in which the basement was the most heavily occupied part. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that or claiming that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you were doing. You were attacking the Vranica building. The forces of the ABiH were concentrated in the basement, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first clash started at the approach to the Vranica building, and the conflict with Vranica started when they started shooting at us from the Vranica building. At the entrance to the command, there were two bunkers, and fire was opened from there. And we already faced each other with a group that was infiltrated along the Rondo area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to who had started the fighting that day, you told the Trial Chamber, in the case in which you gave evidence previously, that you didn't know because you had arrived too late to see for yourself but could only say what you'd been told; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said to us yesterday that you thought you had arrived at about 6.30. It may matter not very much at all, but I want to just be clear. You said, in the last -- on the last occasion on which you testified, that you arrived between 7.00 and as late as 8.00 a.m. that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the reference is page 13.104 of the transcript, which is available in a separate binder, but it may be the witness knows that that's what he said. Perhaps he's had a chance to look at that transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As late as 8.00 that morning was the time that you gave. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember my statement on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's up to an hour and a half later than what you told us yesterday, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I be allowed to explain? If a planned -- if it's a planned operation, then there is a plan of attack, and then I would certainly be able to remember all that. But this way, it is obvious that I intervened, and that is why I cannot say with any certainty what the exact time was. That's why there might be some deviations there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we appreciate --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I'm going to have to correct the transcript once again to avoid some misunderstanding between the Prosecutor and the witness. On page 37, line 6, the witness said, "If the operation had been planned, I would certainly be able to remember the time." And in the record, it says: "... to remember all that." So just to remember the time. The witness can say if I'm right or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, have you listened to what Ms. Tomanovic has just said? She was asking you to confirm what you have said exactly, whether you said "remember all that" or whether you said "remember the time."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said "the time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the break now, because it is 10.30. I would like to tell Mr. Laws that he has 29 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. Mr. Registrar, you have the floor. I believe you have a couple of IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Praljak Defence has submitted its objections to documents tendered by the Prosecution through Witness Vlado Sakic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1079. And the Prosecution has also submitted its objections to documents tendered by the Praljak Defence through the same witness. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1080. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, would you turn, please, to P02240. It's the sixth document in from the beginning of the bundle. It's a document we've already looked at in a different context earlier this morning. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Signed by Miljenko Lasic. It's an order dated the 9th of May of 1993, which says that given the developments in the town of Mostar, an order is being given for a unit of the HVO 4th Stjepan Radic Brigade from Ljubuski should get up at 5.30 on the 10th of May of 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And: "Commanders from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit should deploy the unit at 600 hours." And then, number 3, that: "A unit from the 4th Brigade is to be subordinated to" -- is that you? "Commander Dragan from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit." It looks like it is you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're going to be held responsible for implementing the order. So on the 9th of May, the Ludvig Pavlovic units were certainly part of the battle plan for the city of Mostar; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you said here "in the city of Mostar and pursuant to an action for the defence of the city." Already on the 9th or as early as the 9th, I was already deployed for the -- to defend the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and plans are being made for further units to be subordinated to you on the following day, aren't they? That's what this order is all about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Reinforcements are being called in, more troops are being called in, in order to win the battle. That's what it comes down to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is obvious that the Croatian Defence Council troops were not enough to defend Mostar, and that is why they were calling for other units to assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether it's enough troops to defend Mostar or enough troops to successfully attack and capture Mostar, other people will have to decide. But your deployment, if you were deployed early on the morning of the 9th of May, that would be completely consistent with other occasions when the Ludvig Pavlovic unit had been deployed to shore up an offensive to make good an HVO operation that had been started, wouldn't it? That had happened to you several times in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The -- an example that would be most like this one would be on the 13th of July, when, in early-morning hours, again we were called upon to go and prevent this attack. In -- during an attack, my unit would have preparations, as in this operation, which would take a bit longer because you would have to conduct reconnaissance, organise, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were fighting alongside the Convicts Battalion, were you not --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not fighting alongside or we were not fighting together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Bruno Busic Battalion were also deployed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at P04 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a question for you from this document, and I thank Mr. Laws for having put a question to you on this document because it's essential for me. This document is written by Miljenko Lasic. It's dated May 9th. We don't know at what time, but during the day of May 9. And in this document, he's asking for you to deploy your unit at 6.00 a.m. The 4th Stjepan Radic Brigade will be subordinated to your unit -- to you. And this brigade is supposed to be there as of 5.30 a.m. on May 10; not on May 9, but the next day, on May 10. Please look at the reference on this document. There is a number, "03-0403-1/93." Do you see this reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's assume, and we're assuming, that the HVO did prepare an attack. Preparations must have started on May 8th, maybe even May 7th or May 6th. According to you, do you think that in the log-book, with this reference number 402, 401, 399, 398, don't you think that these documents would refer to an attack order, militarily-wise? Here we have an order 403, but before that, in the log-book, there must be 402, 401, and so forth. So if Lasic is actually preparing this attack, shouldn't we be able to trace the order of attack in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, Your Honour, how the administrative markings worked, but in the military sense it was important whether this was an order or a decision and what it states in the preamble. But as for the numbering and the records, anything I would say about that would be speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that there's always an explanation to an order that you can find in an order, and we do have this explanation in this order that we have here on the screen. There were developments in the town of Mostar in accordance with the action to defend the town, "I issue the following order." I did note this. And when Mr. Laws was putting the question to you, I was wondering the following: I was wondering whether this order was an order following an attack order. But if this had been the case, it should have said, In accordance with the order to attack, I ask you to do this or that. Shouldn't it be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the beginning of this order, we see that it says: "Given the developments in the town of Mostar and in accordance with the action to defend the town." Nowhere does it say an action to attack. It says here "to defend the town," literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It all depends what you mean by "defending," doesn't it? Those words don't mean that the HVO is resisting an ABiH attack in the slightest, do they? The HVO regarded Mostar as its capital, didn't it? Didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've read what's written here, "In accordance with the action to defend the town," so I can't really speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a moment ago about whether you fought side by side with the Convicts Battalion. You said you didn't. But they were involved in the fighting, and you saw Tuta that day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were involved in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second part of the question: You saw Tuta that day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that was on the 9th or the 10th when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the course of those two days, you saw Tuta, and he was part of the fighting in Mostar? Are we agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him in combat. I saw him outside the ministry building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with me that one of the topics that you came to testify about for him, when called in his defence, was that he was not commanding troops in Mostar on the 9th/10th of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you didn't put that question to me, whether he was commanding. You said that he was fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't put that question to you, and I asked whether you recalled that that was a topic that you testified about that, the topic that his Defence wanted to try to establish through you; namely, that Tuta was not a commander. Do you remember that you gave evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, Mr. Prosecutor, but, in fact, the question that you put to me was whether Tuta fought, and I told you that he didn't, that I saw him outside the ministry building. Now, if you ask me some other questions, I'll gladly answer them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've asked you two separate questions: one about whether you saw Tuta fighting; one whether it's right that you gave evidence on behalf of him that he was not a commander of troops. And have you taken the trouble to read what the Trial Chamber made of that assertion, that Tuta was not a commander? Have you had a look at the judgement to see whether they thought you were right about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can help you. It's at paragraph 146 of the judgement, and they reject your testimony that Naletilic did not command any units involved in the attack on Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, as this evidence is inconsistent with the testimonies of the numerous other witnesses. All right? In other words, they do not accept what you said to them; they reject it. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest of respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- these comments, in relation to my friend's last question, is quite appropriate, quite appropriate and permissible at the stage of closing speeches or written submissions; but as far as cross-examination is concerned, it's my respectful submission that it's inappropriate to put to the witness what the view of his testimony was by another Trial Chamber. Of course, what's important is not for this Trial Chamber to abdicate its fact-finding responsibilities to that of another Trial Chamber, but it falls for Your Honours to make an independent determination as to the evidence this witness gives, what's in all credibility or otherwise. So in that respect, it's my submission that the question put forward by my learned friend is not relevant in the present context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: May I reply to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will reply in a minute, Mr. Laws, but personally I want to say something. The conclusions drawn by another Trial Chamber do not commit us. It's not because another Trial Chamber has drawn a conclusion that this Chamber will draw the same conclusion. What is important, Witness, is the following: The Prosecutor is telling you that you said that the commander of the Convicts Battalion was Andabak, but that the Naletilic Trial Chamber did not admit your version of the facts. And the Prosecutor is thus asking you, by quoting the judgement, whether you maintain your position or not. That's it, in a nutshell. So what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I still -- I remain at the same position. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you wanted to reply? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Only to say that when a Trial Chamber has assessed a witness's evidence on a particular topic, measured against the other available evidence, and given a very clear conclusion, that carries some weight and is an entirely appropriate matter to use to impeach a witness's credit.
