What weight it has is for the Trial Chamber to determine, but to say that it has no weight and can't be asked is, in my submission, just wrong. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I agree with you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a reply to my learned colleague. It is my view that a judgement cannot be used as evidence, that it cannot be presented as another evidence. At least that is what the translation was referring to. It says that the Prosecutor, in order to impeach a witness, may use a judgement. But a judgement of this Tribunal may not be used as evidence in cross-examination or when attempting to impeach a witness and undermine their credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on this -- on these matters. I believe that it's not up to us to rule on this right now. We have heard everything, and we will now continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reality of the position is this: that you were prepared to come and give evidence for Tuta because you were loyal to him. You were loyal to him, having fought with him, and owing him, in your view, that loyalty borne of combat. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you knew things, you would know that Mr. Tuta Naletilic and I are neither friends - we certainly aren't good friends - nor am I loyal to him, nor has he ever ordered anything to me. But the main fact is that we are not friends, and I do not owe him any loyalty. And this is something that you can easily verify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have remained loyal to what I'm going to call the Herceg-Bosna project for many years after the end of the conflict, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I have remained loyal to the Croatian people. Everything that is in the interests of the Croatian people, I'm ready to be loyal to, and I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you became, as you told us yesterday, the senior HVO representative in the federation army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not a post that went particularly smoothly for you, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at a few of the highlights of the years in which you occupied that post. Would you turn, please, to P11061. It's six documents in from the back of the binder. From -- no, from the back. 11061. This is an extract from a report by -- the whole of a report from the BBC, dated the 29th of July of 1996. It cites its source as Croat Radio Herceg-Bosna in Mostar, and it's an excerpt from a report by Bosnian Croat Radio on the 26th of July. And you can read for yourself what it says, Mr. Curcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the article have it right that new recruits swore an oath of allegiance to Herceg-Bosna in 1996 with you present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, Mr. Prosecutor. I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, try and help us. Did they swear an oath of allegiance at the military base in Capljina, as it says in the second paragraph, promising to carry out the Croat soldiers' duties with honour, defend the country, their Croat people, and all citizens of the self-proclaimed Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Did they take an oath of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you with certainty. I was present. But if they swore allegiance, I don't see anything wrong with that, if that is the case, as they claim here. But I really can't remember what that oath of allegiance -- what the wording was at the time. And if you have the text of the oath with you, perhaps it would be a good idea to see it, the oath of allegiance of 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need the text of the oath of allegiance to be able to tell us whether that paragraph has it broadly right. Not the exact words, but is it broadly right that they, for example, pledged to defend the country, the Croat people, and all citizens of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna? That's all I'm asking you. Is that the sort of thing that happened in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is certain that there must be at least five different versions of the text of the oath of allegiance. I don't know which one would have been used here. If this was the one that was used, I agree, but I really don't know, and I cannot confirm this. But we can easily get a copy from some organs, but I really cannot know exactly whether it was the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, or Herceg-Bosna, or whatever it said in the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of the five versions that you are familiar with, was such an oath included? Is that a yes-or-no answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. There was a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; there was the federation army, that was a separate oath; and now we have the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn over, please, two documents to P11063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the date of July 29, 1996, well, I'm trying to place this in relation to the Washington Agreements. In July 1996, was the conflict over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conflict is over. Why is it that in the attendance list there are no representative of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? They're not mentioned. Why is that? There is mention of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, of HVO, of the Croatian Army, of municipalities, of the parents, relatives, but there's no official representative from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it because the journalist forgot to mention it, or, as far as you recollect, were they not invited, or maybe they declined to come? They did come, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they did not come. At that time and up until 2000 something, whenever there were celebrations of the Croatian Defence Council, there were representatives from the ministry, Croats; but when there were some celebrations of the BH Army, there were only representatives from the ministry, Bosniak representatives. And only after 2001 or 2002 did it come about that both the sides would attend the events of either partner. And today, all three sides actually attend, because the Serb part also became part of the federation. But at this time, immediately following the war, this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask you a difficult question. You might not remember. But regarding this ceremony for new soldiers, did you invite the BH Army, and they would have declined to come, but did you invite them; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not invite them; they did not invite us. We did not attend their events; they did not attend ours. This only came about after joint institutions were set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn, from the document you've been looking at just now, 11061, another page to 11062. We'll look at that one first. It's another document in time. It's another report from the BBC, and it apparently comes from a news agency in Zagreb. And it's another short report under the heading "USA Reportedly Wants Sacking of Croat Opponents." Just have a read of those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading document 11063?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, 062. It's good that you've read that, we're coming to that as well, but 062.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It concerns the delays that had occurred in establishing the federation army. Is the report right, that the Muslims wanted integrated units and that the HVO did not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true in the sense where it's not explained that they wanted to have integrated units, but in which they would be the dominant partner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was the United States government right to blame you and others for these delays?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then turn the page, please, to 11063. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're answering very quickly, but the US government or any -- when the US government or any government says something, they don't say it lightly. They usually have first-hand information. And here you are being challenged directly. In this document, it says that you are being -- that you're against the creation of this federal army. You are being personally challenged. According to you, are the Americans wrong? Were they poorly informed? How can you explain that the US government is blaming you directly, but today you're saying that it's not true? How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are many documents and decisions where my work is applauded because I participated in the programme called "Train and Exercise," and for the work in the Federation; but these events came about at the time when the Croatian self-determination was attempted, so a large number of Croat representatives were sacked, also the Croatian member of the Presidency, as well as some other things that occurred then. And at that time, I left the army, but Mr. Prce, and I participated in a very constructive manner in the programme "Equip and Train" and in the establishment of a joint force. As for this opinion that is put forward here, I really can't say anything about it. I don't know what the reason for that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the following year, then. If you turn the page again to 11063, the document that I think you were reading a few moments ago, in this document we learn that some 2.000 Bosnian Croat soldiers had deserted the Bosnian Muslim Croat Federation in support of Croat separatists. They paraded at a local stadium in Mostar in a new act of defiance, and that you reviewed the troops. They were unarmed, but wore the uniforms, minus the insignia of the Muslim Croat Federation. Does that accurately record the events of May the 11th of 2001, when you reviewed those troops?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you come down the page, we have a paragraph which says: "Most of the seven and a half thousand Croat troops serving with the Muslim Croat Federations Army deserted in mid-March, siding with Bosnian Croat nationalists who proclaimed temporary autonomy within Bosnia." And then it goes on to say that over a quarter of them have since gone back. You were allied to those who wanted to achieve autonomy within Bosnia for Herceg-Bosna, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with the majority. As you can see here, it's the majority. And throughout the time, we fought for the rights of the Croatian people. And as for the other matters, that's a bit more general, and I can't speak to that because I'm not a politician. But there was an attempt at this time to abrogate -- to cut back on some rights of the Croatian people, and of course --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would appreciate the witness repeating the last portion of his reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, the interpreters asked you to repeat the second part of your answer. Please repeat it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as it says here, I sided with a huge majority that wanted to protect the Croatian people. And they wanted the protection of the Croatian people within the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you turn over to P11064, a report by AFP from the 15th of March of 2001, please take a moment to read that, Mr. Curcic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It quotes Ante Jelavic as having some comments to make about Croat self-rule. He was an associate of yours, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Jelavic was a member of the Presidency. He was the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ally yourself with him, politically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I allied with the people. As you can see here, I offered my resignation because I wanted to remain loyal to the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're right, that is recorded there, that you wanted to remain loyal to the Croatian people. And in your view, did Mr. Jelavic want the same as you, to remain loyal to the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelavic was tried in Sarajevo for these things, and you can see the judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't, with respect to you, quite answer the question that I just asked. Did Mr. Jelavic want the same as you, to remain loyal to the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Witness, perhaps you can ask him -- counsel, I apologise, but I believe that this answer will lead to further unnecessary questions. But the witness clearly said in Croatian that Jelavic -- or, I apologise. That was on page 53, line 23, that Jelavic had been tried in Sarajevo and acquitted, and this did not enter the transcript. So Jelavic was acquitted, and that is not something that was reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is a correction that I have to make here. Jelavic was not acquitted, but he was tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the Jelavic trial for him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I believe Ms. Nozica would be better acquainted with that because she was one of the participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter for our purposes at all what he was tried for and why, what the outcome was. What he was saying and doing is what I'm interested in. And I want to know if you shared his views and shared his aspirations for autonomy, for an autonomous entity in Bosnia. Is that what you wanted in 2001, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was always on the side of the Croatian people, loyal to them. Mr. Jelavic was a politician. And as to his conduct, I cannot have any final opinion about that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, had I asked you about his conduct, that would be an answer. Just -- I'll read it to you again. I want to know if you shared his views and shared his aspirations for autonomy, for an autonomous entity in Bosnia. Is that what you wanted in 2001, Mr. Curcic, an autonomous entity in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were the possibility of having a state for the Croatian people, then that's what I would like best, but there isn't. And you keep asking me the same thing, whereas in this interview I offered my resignation -- I am answering. I said what I would like and to whom I was loyal and am loyal, the Croatian people and their interests. And I make no mention of any -- well, the kind of things that Mr. Jelavic is talking about. I can say what my wishes are, and I wish the Croats all the best, to have a state which would be the richest in the world, but it is impossible under the present conditions or under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was what you were fighting for in 1993 as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know what I mean. For an independent state within Bosnia for Croats. That's what you were fighting for then, and that's what you've told us you would still like now, if you could do it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, had the objectives of the war been defined of any of the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war began, that is, then that war would not have been that bloody or that brutal. However, the objectives, even if they existed, I did not know of them. But under number 1, we had the protection of my nation, of which I am a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are not listening to the questions that are being put to you. The Prosecutor is putting to you a crucial question. He is telling you that you fought for an independent state. You need to answer this question, say either yes or no. And there is no answer for the time being. Let me pick up on the Prosecutor's question. Did you fight for an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fought for my own people. For what state, the Croats, the Bosniaks, which?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You fought for your people. Explain this to me, then. You resigned, and you told us why. When a multi-ethnic army was being set up together with Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and you then resign. I find it difficult to understand why you resigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. At the time, there were no Serbs there integrated into the joint armed forces, only the Bosniaks and Croats or, rather, component parts of the HVO and the BH Army. It was only in 2005, or whenever, was this integrated into the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where we had the members of the Army of Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having specified that. But at the time you resigned, an army was being set up that comprised both the Croats and the Muslims, and we know, because we have heard evidence on this, sometimes you were fighting alongside the Serbs. This army is, therefore, being set up. Why do you leave? That is what the Prosecutor is trying to elicit from you. Why did you leave? Did you leave because this didn't coincide with the idea you had of the political institutions that were about to be set up, because you wanted an independent state which you weren't getting, so that's why you resigned; or you left for another reason? The Prosecutor is trying to find out why, like the Bench is, for that matter, as well. We're all trying to understand why it is you left. And you are the person concerned here because you are the person who resigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was one of the people who established the army of the Federation from 1997 up until the time when I left Sarajevo, and I was certainly one of the most deserving people in building up a joint army of the Federation during those four or five years, which was the time I spent in Sarajevo. Now, when the electoral laws were passed which were contrary to the interests of the Croatian people, then all the structures and all the people, all the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, stood up, arose, because by those new electoral laws we would have lost our constituent character. And that's when the whole Croatian entity and soul started -- was stirred up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, because -- this new electoral law triggered your resignation. Why didn't you say it right from the start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the electoral law was unfavorable, as far as the Croats were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have 3 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not all Croats shared your view, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't possibly claim to speak for all Croats.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't claim that, either. I'm speaking on behalf of the majority, as it says here in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your goal, as you've told us, was autonomy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our goal was to enable equal rights to the Croats as the other two nations or ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you agreed that you expressed a preference for the solution of an independent Croat entity a few moments ago. Do you want to change your mind about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said it in the sense of wishes, if wishes could be -- could come true, could be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the end game, Mr. Curcic, wasn't just to have a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was Croatian, but to join up with Croatia. That's the bottom line here, isn't it? That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't always understand you, in your efforts and endeavours, to know what I'm thinking better than I do, myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been heavily involved in a movement for many years, and I'm putting to you what its final goal was. To join up with the paymasters, the people who were paying your wages all the time you were travelling around Bosnia, fighting against the legitimate army of that country, that's the goal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if there was the possibility, if the possibility existed, then all Croats would like to see that, but there is no realistic possibility for that within the frameworks of all the events that were happening. So the reality is Bosnia-Herzegovina, with respect for all ethnic groups and giving all ethnic groups and nations the same rights. Now, at that time it was the vital interests of the Croatian nation that were under threat. It's not only I who say that; the media wrote about it and talked about it. And just as these people are writing bad things about us, so also there were positive writings saying that some rights of the Croatian people should be fulfilled, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the obstacles in the way of you achieving that goal back in 1993 was the fact that the area that had proclaimed itself as Herceg-Bosna had a very substantial Muslim population. That was the problem back then, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The problem with achieving your desired solution of breaking away from the republic and joining Croatia was that that was not a solution that attracted the substantial Muslim population of Herceg-Bosna. That was the problem, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The problem -- the general problem in 1993 was that there were many enclaves, Croatian enclaves, in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, the area controlled by the Croats was separated, they didn't have any connection between them. And that was the major problem. Now, as far as the Muslim population is concerned, I told you how many remained in Mostar. I don't know the exact number, but I do know that a large number did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you that the solution to that problem that was adopted, for example, in Capljina was simply rounding them up at gunpoint, putting them on buses, and shipping them out to areas that you didn't claim. That was the solution that was adopted, and it was a solution you knew full well about, as your letter about Fatima Klepo makes clear. That's the truth, isn't it, Mr. Curcic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to help Ms. Klepo. Now, what you say, you keep saying that the truth is that I know, I knew. I don't know. What I knew and what I know is what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So redirect. As far as the Praljak Defence is concerned, do you have any redirect for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we do. I'm going to have more corrections to the transcript. I didn't want to interrupt the cross-examination. So I have two questions, and Mr. Praljak also has some questions related to military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, General, I'd like to start off with the following. While we still have the page on our screens, I'd like to ask you the following. The Prosecutor's question was formulated in the following way. He said: You travelled around Bosnia and you fought against the legitimate army of that country, and that was your goal, to fight against the legitimate army of the country? Is that true and correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. The legitimate army, well, the legitimate army was the HVO which, according to all the laws in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was confirmed, because the same rights were realised by members of the HVO and the BH Army. But I didn't hear him ask the question that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not, but it was recorded on page 58, lines 19 to 23. Similarly, in yesterday's transcript your answer was recorded, and as you were gesticulating while you were giving your answer, the transcript isn't quite clear in that portion. So I'd like to focus on page 37, lines 5 to 10, and it relates to a question that Ms. Alaburic put to you linked to documents 4D0618 and P7419. Now, my question to you, linked to those two documents, is the following: The ATG Tvrtko, the ATG from Livno, and other ATGs, were they within the same structure as Ludvig Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tvrtko ATG was not, nor was Livno in the same structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So what units, along with Ludvig Pavlovic, were in the same structure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same structure, you had Bruno Busic, the Vitezovi, Ludvig Pavlovic, the Convicts Battalion of 92, and the Baja Kraljevic ATG.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on page 100, line 1, of yesterday's transcript, your answer was recorded. I think it was wrongly recorded, but let me ask you the question because I don't want to suggest an answer to you. Ludvig Pavlovic, your unit, had under its control a large territory of the HZ-HB or was active over a large territory of HZ-HB; which?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was of the manoeuvre type, and it acted over a large territory. It did not control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And once again a correction to today's transcript, your answer recorded on page 61, line 19 and 20. The Convicts Battalion was within the structure of -- when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion was in the structure in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Or perhaps the Usher can put P02240, the next document, on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We discussed the document several times today. It's an order stating that a unit from the 4th HVO Brigade, on the 10th of May, should be -- should get up and be awakened at 5.30. Does that mean that the whole brigade was to arrive in Mostar, was to go to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did the unit reach Mostar on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not report to me. Now, whether they arrived or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That means you didn't do anything with them, you didn't deploy them at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deploy them according to this order because they didn't report to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And another document discussed today. The Prosecutor showed you document P9847, and he referred to page 3 of that document. And what was suggested to you was that in Mostar, in West Mostar, no Muslims remained. Now, as we're dealing with redirect --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's simply not right. This document has nothing to do with Mostar. It's to do with Stolac-Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry, but page 3 refers to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I didn't put page 3 to the witness. That's all. I put page 2, so far as it relates to the 13th of July, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that same page, above that paragraph beginning: "On the 13th of July ...," so on that same page, above "the 13th of July," it says -- I beg your pardon. My mistake. 13th of June. I do apologise. I was looking at the wrong date, the 13th of June. Never mind. We'll skip that. However, the Prosecutor, nevertheless, suggested to the witness that the Muslims were expelled from West Mostar, because the witness's answer was that, to the best his recollections, there were a certain number of Muslims who stayed on in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So I'd like to see P5984, please, the next document. It is -- did I give the wrong number there? I don't know which number you mean. 5984, P5984. P -- P5984. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Look at the document, please. Can you see it on your screens?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: According to this document, in Mostar, in October 1993, were there any Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the figure there is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8.100 -- I'm reading the total number. Is that what you want? 8.141.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the table relates to whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- these are parts of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what population there, which inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Retired? It said "retirees"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 20th of October, 1993, there were that many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes my portion of the cross-examination -- or re-examination, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Before we leave that document, it's not a document that was used in the course of the cross-examination at all, and -- I don't dispute that at all, but the witness has just been asked to confirm something. The document appears to give us columns, and we appear to have in evidence that it shows there are 8.141 Muslims in total. Perhaps that is what it says, but it isn't remotely clear to me; and how it's clear to the witness, I don't know, either. It appears to say different numbers as we go across, and the figure for Muslims looks like it's 2.107. So I just want the record to be clear as to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second column refers to Muslim Bosniaks, retired persons. Your Honours, with your permission, General Praljak would now like to ask several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let me remind you that in your redirect you must put questions that refer to questions put by Mr. Laws in his cross-examination. Otherwise, Mr. Laws is going to raise objections all the time. So now you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm quite sure that I won't move outside the frameworks of what the Prosecutor asked, and I don't think he'll have any objections to make in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Curcic, good morning to you once again.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Kralj Tomislav is a regiment which was established where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kralj Tomislav is a regiment founded in Croatia, in Dubrovnik and then in Vrgorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you were the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That particular unit, how many Croats were there in it and how many Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit had 60 per cent Croats and about 40 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What percentage of people in that unit was born on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and was citizens of the republic or, rather, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina just like you are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 90 per cent of the members were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you a military conscript of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an active military person in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well, we know that. But afterwards, you were a military conscript of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I stayed on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct. Now, the Prosecutor said the Croatian Army -- you were on loan. He used the term "on loan." You said that was a strange term to use. But isn't it correct to say that you were on loan from Bosnia-Herzegovina, both the Croats and Bosniaks, voluntarily to the Croatian Army to defend the south of Croatia? Would that be a more correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We first went to defend Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, Cepikuce, did you take part in the fighting for Cepikuce?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me, General, but members of our unit, yes, led by the late Bozan Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Against whom were you fighting in Cepikuce?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fought there against the Serb army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, it doesn't matter whether you were there, personally. I'm talking about the unit. Now, had Cepikuce been lost at the time, where would the Serb -- what area would the Serb army have reached and what axis would it have taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Cepikuce fallen, automatically Dubrovnik would have fallen, and they would have advanced to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your commander, you say that your commander was General Daidza; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What was his full name, his real name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all knew him under the name of Mate Sarlija, nicknamed Daidza, but his real name was Nijaz Batlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, please, after the truce that was signed, as far as Croatia is concerned, where did you have your training centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our training centres in Basko Polje and Vrgorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who came from Bosnia-Herzegovina to be trained in your training centres, to be trained and go back? Were they Croats, Bosniaks? Were there more Croats than Bosniaks or more Muslims than Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prevailing number was among the Bosniaks. There were more Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What was the name of the logistics man in your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kralj Tomislav logistics man was Nikica Raguz -- Nikica Raguz and Marko Potrebica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as you know, how many weapons were sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina via Kralj Tomislav unit? That's the first question. And how much of those -- how many of those weapons were sent to the Muslims and how many to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, General. There were large quantities, we are talking about truckloads here, but most of those weapons went to the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, can we agree that Mr. Nijaz Batlak or Mate Sarlija was a Croatian general, a general of the Croatian Army, and that he provided weapons in truckloads that were sent to the army -- or, rather, to the Muslims of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did Zuka also come for training to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zuka was in Basko Polje with us for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We all know here who Zuka was, so we won't dwell on that any longer. Now, my next question. Following this, what happened was an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, the JNA and the Serbian Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before we go on to that, could we please have document 3D00420. 3D00420. As you can see, this is a document from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it relates to a decision on the formation of Territorial Defence units. And you can see, under 1, that the person who signed this document, and as we will see, this will -- we will see in a moment that this was Alija Izetbegovic, well, where we see that he proclaims Kralj Tomislav unit and General Mate Sarlija as a Bosnian-Herzegovinian brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a question from the Chamber. The document is interesting, but was this mentioned in the cross-examination? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the foundation for the questioning was the status of the brigade Kralj Tomislav or, rather, the regiment, where we see an order that Mate Sarlija, Daidza, is the commander, and the basis of that was to show that the Croatian Army -- that actually it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina under the orders of the Croatian Army. But from this document, Your Honours, we can see that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic considers that brigade to be a brigade of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he considers Mate Sarlija, Daidza, a commander of his Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that he actually appoints him to that position. In other words, he appoints him as commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I may well stand to be corrected, but I don't think I asked any questions about the Kralj Tomislav Brigade at all at any stage, and I hope I've been quite patience, watching the transcript going by, but we haven't been dealing with topics that arose in cross-examination now for some few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think that really a response is needed. The transcript could easily show whether this brigade was discussed or not. And if I may add, since I'm on my feet, this is a classical example how documents and which kind of documents should be used on direct. Mr. Praljak precisely said what was inserted in the cross and precisely said why this document has to be shown in redirect. This is more than a clear example. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's sure is that General Daidza was a topic mentioned by the Prosecutor. It seems that the real name of Daidza was Mate Sarlija and that we have a document mentioning him within the army -- the BH Army. Let's move on. Please put your question, General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is very simple. Sir, are you aware -- do you know that at this time you were, in fact, under the command both of Alija Izetbegovic and the Croatian Army, as this document shows?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point, there was a clash in the army, the conflict broke out; and this brigade, this regiment, Kralj Tomislav, in view of its composition, crossed over to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to fight for the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it true that it was split into two: A, Ludvig Pavlovic, numbering 92 members; and another number of Muslims who went to Konjic to create what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To establish the regiment Nihad Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Nihad Kulenovic was part of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Of the original 92 members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Regiment, how many were Croats and how many Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but the ratio is about 70 to 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that these members, too, who had gone to join the Konjic Regiment, which was part of the BH Army, were they, too, retained -- or did they, too, retain the status as Croatian soldiers when their benefits are concerned and their pay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it true that the 92 of you also retained that status?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, General. The Prosecutor showed you a good number of documents earlier. We spent a lot of time on this. But now I'm discovering that the soldiers who had left the Republic of Croatia to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina were split up in two. Some joined your Ludvig Pavlovic unit, and the others go to Konjic to join a BH Army regiment, the Nihad Kulenovic Brigade. Now, I'd like to know the following: The soldiers that go to the BH Army, as far as you know, were they still paid by the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even General Daidza, in his case, he spent more time in Konjic than in Croatia or Herzegovina. In other words, they retained their rights, just like the 92 of us did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, General Daidza came to see you and then would go and visit the Muslim soldiers in the BH Army. He would go from one unit to the other; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. It was only on the 6th of June that the Ludvig Pavlovic unit was established. Up until then, we were part of Kralj Tomislav, and I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, could you tell us whether the Muslim soldiers in the BH Army who were stationed in Konjic were still -- were they still paid by the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know because at that time we had lost contact, we were not in contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Curcic, do you recall that you addressed me as well within the Ministry of the Republic of Croatia relating -- regarding the status and service-related matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, we addressed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request, could the question please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. General, would you please slow down a bit. A portion of your question, which is important, did not make it into the transcript. On page 72, lines 7 to 9, the General said that both sides addressed him, requesting assistance to resolve the status-related and service-related issues, and I would really appreciate it if the general could repeat his question because the transcript is unclear as it stands. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, did you address me in the Ministry of the Republic of Croatia to resolve the status and service-related issues of the 92 of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And also the issues that related to the men who had joined the regiment in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, would I, perhaps, be the best source to provide an answer about the date up until when all the members of Kralj Tomislav who were members of the Croatian Army, regardless of whether later on they joined the HVO or the BH Army, up until what date they actually enjoyed the benefits of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think that would be you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We saw that Mr. Nijaz Batlak was appointed, and this was his real name of Mato Sarlija, that he was appointed by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that he received his pension, once he retired, from the Croatian Army and that he was buried at Mirogoj as a member of -- as a Croatian general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at Mirogoj. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we now see 3D00560. 3D00560.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please read this document. I don't know if you have ever seen the signature of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, but I think you had occasion to see it in Sarajevo. My question is this: Do you know that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic trusted, to a large extent, and had intimate cooperation with General Daidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them personally together, but Mr. Izetbegovic's envoys often came to see General Daidza in Vrgorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic wanted to entrust the operation for the liberation of Sarajevo to General Daidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was this operation carried out? And we won't discuss how successfully.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more an attempt at doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did members of Kralj Tomislav participate in this attempt?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the last question regarding this: When you were -- when you crossed over to the HVO, was it voluntary or did you ever receive an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the easiest -- that's very easy to answer. We went back home. It was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Curcic, other than Bozan Simovic, your commander, who was killed in an operation, was there another commander of your battalion who was killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ante Primorac was killed Kupres during an operation to liberate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify that issue. Did you -- let's talk about Urina Ravan and those events, we were together at that hut. Were we exposed? Could we have been killed because there was shooting going on some 30 metres away from us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you have been killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell us, is it true that the most important thing then was not death, itself, but what would happen to the families; in other words, to your mother, to your father, to your two sisters, what would happen to them after you get killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So Croatia was already a state. Was it important, very important, to gain in any way possible a status so that the Croatian Army would take care of your family and your loved ones if anything should happen to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the most important question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My next question, Mostar. We've seen a document there. Could we see it again, please? This is P02240. While we are waiting for the document to come up, tell us, you have graduated from the Military Academy in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when a military action of an offensive character is being prepared, tell the Trial Chamber, please, briefly, what has to be done before an operation of that type.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, the easiest way would be to describe it if we -- if you -- if we tell you about an order for an operation for attack. The first thing is an assessment. You have to assess the strength, the combat disposition, the possibility of bringing in reserve forces, if possible determining the firing position of the artillery, and so on and so forth. In other words, before any offensive operation is to be conducted, you need to have very high-quality reconnaissance conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise, but both the generals should slow down. I think you're making it very hard for the interpreters. Now, on page 75, line 22, the witness said "assessment of the enemy." That word is missing there, because the interpreters either didn't hear you or didn't have time to interpret you, but can you tell me if I'm right? Did you say "assessment of the enemy"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "assessment of the enemy" is what I said. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it true, General, sir, that maps were drawn up at the time or maps were drawn up at that point, that there's a general plan of attack which is then elaborated down the line among the individual units, that the start of an attack is elaborated, fire support to the artillery, the system of communications and signals is looked at, and everything else, what we call the wounded, where the wounded and casualties are to be collected; so it requires a whole lot of organisation, the necessary ammunition must be put in place and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct that in a large-scale operation -- or let me ask you this first: The taking of Eastern Mostar, and the line was established -- the front-line was along the Bulevar and Santic Street, so taking a town like that defended by the 4th Corps of the BH Army is a major, large-scale operation, or is it a small operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an enormous operation, too large. And I just want to say that the most difficult form of combat that is studied at military academies is combat in built-up areas, in settlements. So any logical soldier belonging to any side would try to avoid fighting in built-up areas because you have special characteristics of warfare there. You don't have a front; you don't have any neighbours. Every building is a bunker, and so on and so forth. And the history of warfare from Stalingrad onwards have always shown that to be true. Then you have Vukovar as another example, and so on and so forth. In Iraq, for example, the troops had problems when entering urban environments; but when they had a clear-cut front in the desert, that was another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And one more thing. Every operation of this kind, does it need reserves? Do you have to create reserves, because the front-line units will suffer from fatigue and then you have to have reserve forces in preparation to replace them; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this: Would it then be possible for an elite unit, of the type that the HVO Main Staff had at its disposal, was asleep, as the Prosecutor says, on the night before a prepared attack against the BH Army in Mostar? Is that something you could envisage at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Secondly, once you arrive in Mostar, you say that the first engagement that you had, the first piece of firing with the BH Army, was at the Rondo area. Now, tell Their Honours where Rondo is located in relation to the Bulevar, which was the separation line already established. So how far is it in to the western side? And take it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rondo is at a distance of 500 metres from that line, and from the Vranica building itself, perhaps 700, thereabouts, and that conflict and the engagement line was not at Rondo, itself, but halfway between Rondo and the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Militarily viewed, was that an incursion by the BH Army towards the HVO; that is to say, movements towards the Ministry of Defence and movements towards Vranica, which is where the Command of the 4th Corps was and the Command of the 1st Brigade of the BH Army, the 1st Mostar Brigade, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let's look at this next document, please. Well, we've already looked at it, and we've seen many similar documents of that nature. Is it possible for a good unit from Ljubuski, for example, does not take part in the attack or was not a reserve force, if someone was preparing an operation to take control of Mostar, would that be possible, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be possible if they had enough forces in some of the operations of attack, but if you had such a broad front, because the town itself, as a town, it would be more probable that it would have been prepared several days in advance and not to have the order issued today for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And do you know, General, that at the time in Mostar, at the northern part of Mostar, facing the Serbs, and the south of Mostar, facing the Serbs, that two brigades -- two HVO brigades, the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades, were engaged, deployed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it the 1st or 2nd? No, the 2nd and 3rd, the 2nd and 3rd, that's the right number. Now, in view of the troops that the HVO brigade had, was it possible, with two brigades which also held the lines facing the Serbs, was it possible to go into any relevant logical operation to take control of the town or, rather, the 4th Corps and the 1st -- let me repeat. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I will slow down, and I do apologise. The devil take me. I apologise to the interpreters. I get carried away. I apologise to Your Honours, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, is it possible, with two HVO brigades, with the number of men that they had, of the strength they had, holding the lines simultaneously facing the Army of Republika Srpska, and to the north of Mostar, and to the south of Mostar, was it militarily possible, having two brigades of this type in Mostar, an inhabited area, to attack the 4th BH Army Corps and reap any success? Is that possible? Are there any realistic foundations for anything like that or is that something just a madman could think up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we're done with that. I just have a few more points. General, do you know that the Croatian people, of their own free will, at a referendum in the spring of 1993, of their own free will, I repeat, voted for an independent, autonomous, integral Bosnia-Herzegovina? In 1992, I meant to say, in 1992. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's leave wishes aside and fantasy aside. But you, as a commander in a mixed unit in Croatia and Bosnia, did you fight for, number 1, protecting Bosnia-Herzegovina against an attack by the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: As I claim, after an attack by the BH Army in the spring of 1993 and then later, were you mostly on the defensive or almost exclusively on the defensive, compared to the attacks Neretva 93, Bugojno, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, in the military sense, and in the general sense, popular sense, did you ever, you, personally, or did you hear from someone, from me or from anybody else, that you wanted in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the Croatian people, anything more than equality, the kind of equality that a sovereign constituent people merit along with other ethnic groups inhabiting the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you want anything other than that, anything else, anything more than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any instructions or orders from anyone, or any considerations, which would indicate something other than the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and equality for the Croatian people, complete equality, full equality of the Croatian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with the other constituent ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN CURCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received an order of that kind or any instructions to that effect. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. General, sir, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your testimony has just come to an end. I will, therefore, ask the Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. I wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as our further hearings are concerned, the Trial Chamber has issued a decision concerning the expert witness. I encourage you and invite you to read this decision. The Trial Chamber has decided that the Defence teams will have four hours for the examination-in-chief, the other Defence teams will have two hours for their cross-examination, and the Prosecutor will have six hours. This is what I wish to tell you, the time it takes to have this translated in your working language. Our decision was recorded yesterday afternoon. Ms. Alaburic, this witness will be ready for Monday, the 26th of October, from 4.00 onwards. It's 4.00 p.m., because prior to that we will shall proceed with the elections of the President of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, the witness is due to come in that week, and he will be ready to appear in court on the 26th. Now, according to our schedule, we said that we would have an introductory section of about an hour and a half, and I wanted to ask you the following, and this is important for the organisation of the first day: This introductory presentation will be prepared following examples and guide-lines given by what Judge Trechsel said, that it should show the Trial Chamber, in the basic forms, of what the topic of the Defence -- topics of the Defence are, and that this should be elaborated with key documents and the subject matter that witnesses will be dealing with. So we're prepared to have an introductory presentation of that kind. Now, if the Trial Chamber has any questions to ask after that introductory presentation has been delivered which you think will speed up our presentation of evidence and examination of witnesses, I will be ready and willing to respond to those questions. And in that case, the following scenario could be put in place: that we begin proceedings at 4.00 in the afternoon with an introductory presentation, which will take up about an hour and a half. After that, we'll have a 20-minute break, which means that we would continue proceedings at around 6.00 p.m. Now, if the Trial Chamber can predict certain questions, I think it would be rational not to introduce the witness into the courtroom late on Monday evening, but to start with the witness on Tuesday morning. But, of course, I don't mind having the witness ready and waiting to come into the courtroom at 6.00 p.m. if you feel that would be opportune. That's what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, if I have understood you correctly, you had rather present your introduction for an hour and a half in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you have finished with that, we shall have the break, and around 6.00 p.m. we can ask the witness to take the solemn declaration and start with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll do that, Your Honour. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That satisfies the Chamber. The most important point, in our eyes, was that of the expert witness whom we would like to hear. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Just to be absolutely clear, because sometimes there is confusion based on different practices, when Ms. Alaburic says "introductory presentation," we're talking about an opening statement, the sort that the Prosecution gave and the sort that other counsel have given. We're talking about an opening statement, not evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is indeed an opening statement, and in future I'm going to use English terms when referring to something that is important to us. So the opening statement will take an hour and a half, and that opening statement will be delivered by me, as lead counsel for General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On a personal note, Ms. Alaburic, it is of interest, because with your opening statement we will be able to get an insight in those questions you will put to the witness and assess the witness's report, so this is a very good idea. We will see, in practice, how this works on Monday, the 26th. In the meantime, I hope to see you on the 26th, the Monday afternoon, and we can all read and examine the witness's report. The court stands adjourned.
